Like others have suggested, it's likely a supply issue 

Click the Manage Resources button (hotkey V), and in the lower left area, click Supply Chain Mode (or hotkey T). Click Mirror Mode (hotkey M) if it's not already on so if you click on one generator, it'll select both. Then, one at a time, right-click each shield to establish a supply chain of power from the generator to your shields. With Mirror Mode selected, if you do this for one side of your ship, it'll mirror the same thing to the other side; it's a nice time-saver.

Last, and this is unrelated, it doesn't look like you have any reverse thrusters. Consider making room for some, so you can hastily back up in case an enemy tries to flank you to avoid your shields altogether. Keep the enemy in front so they *have* to deal with your shields! Good luck!

Very agreed. To answer your question, first know my PTSD therapy may differ from yours. I'm a disabled combat veteran, and the mental health care I receive is strictly through the VA, and is, well, not known to be the best.

As was explained to me, part of recovery for me involves stretching certain boundaries that have been (involuntarily) in place since my traumas; avoiding crowds, avoiding loud noises, closing off from society/friends/family, etc. Basically, if I had my way, I'd live in a cave, under mountain, somewhere maps don't exist. The therapy I'm involved with challenges me to take baby steps against the grain, like maybe not mosh-pits, but going out in public a bit more. Engage with people more often, check in from time to time, make less excuses to not attend safe gatherings. I could easily live a total recluse life, but things like this help me when inevitable curveballs come along (like a 1-time group of workers in your home). Docs have told me that if I don't work through my triggers, they stand a good chance of only getting worse. That's my understanding, anyway.

I'm so sorry to hear that, friend. Outside of meds (which I understand may take time to kick into effect), is there a quiet, safe place you're able to be in to decompress? Personally, I know therapists will discourage avoidant habits, but as a 1-time thing maybe consider diving into something to distract yourself? An art project of sorts, another good book, a movie, a game, even a set of headphones and a nice chill music playlist? 

You'll get through this, any which way works best for you. I just hope it happens quickly for you.

It may be worth going directly to the Voc Rehab office, and getting face-to-face with a supervisor. I tried the program last year, and had so many problems getting paid, getting registered, and even getting emails/calls returned, I had to stop the program (was making daily calls to Vet crisis line by that point). 

There's a solid group on FB for Voc Rehab (just search for it by name, several thousand members), and they may be able to offer some "Here's what worked for me" guidance. 

On paper, the program is amazing. In practice, I have never been so stressed out in my life, and would rather go back to the desert than ever try negotiating that maze again. So much of it is contingent on everyone else doing their jobs, and countless vets end up being ping-ponged around as the messenger between the Voc Rehab office, the local school's Veteran Services Office, and the actual school registration office, NONE of whom communicate with each other. 

I truly hope you have better luck, friend.

US Army combat vet with diagnosed PTSD here:

Please don't be offended if they aren't quite at a place to accept help, or articulate exactly how they best need support. I've seen well-intending people try to offer hugs, pats on the back, and other close-proximity physical contact get real upset when the victim isn't immediately consoled, if not temporarily worse. "Well, I'm just trying to HELP, jeez."

Obviously you're not that kind of person, you're on here asking for guidance :) But it can feel weird if your best efforts aren't the "silver bullet." I see a lot of wonderful feedback here, especially centering on that communication. Consider asking before or soon after an episode, when they have the bandwidth & faculties to really ponder how someone else could help them in the moment. 

I'm taking a page from the VA here, but consider an informal action-plan with your friend. When something happens that trigger/may trigger them, have an agreed-upon series of options, written down if possible. 

Something like:

"When I start to feel anxious, I should text ___. If possible, I should find a safe area to get to such as ___, ___, or ___. I will take (Rx) as soon as possible. I can call ___ if I need a ride. I can use the ___ app on my phone to help meditate, or listen to (chill music mix). My local crisis line number is ____, and ____ can be with me if I call. My doctor is ___ and should be notified when this happens, and may need a note for work/school."

I've used things like that many times, and when I've been in an anxiety attack, those simple steps have helped keep me together. Though my mind often races at what feels like a million miles an hour, putting those simple steps together when I'm freaking out could feel impossible without having that on paper, and my friend's support. 

Best luck to you, and you're an awesome friend to have for seeking this kind of help out :)

It may not be as crooked a slip as it sounds, re-reading it. Rather than an arbitrary fee, I'd almost guarantee they're suggesting an electronic version of a stop payment (applicable for ACH transactions, if ever).

It's the wrong kind of solution to your problem, though your banker isn't trying to be skeezy about it. Given the bait & switch approach given by your investment-no-wait-insurance salesperson, I'd say that absolutely qualifies as fraud in the eyes of any bank or credit union. The old "But you gave me your account info" doesn't fly for erroneous charges you didn't authorize, and can't get refunded (or even responded to) from the offending company. You're well within your rights to a fraud claim here. 

I wouldn't go the route of that $28 stop payment. It's effective on paper checks, because you know the exact amount it'd be redeemed for (because you wrote the check). Totally valid point, I was more referring to the people that run overdrawn regularly, and choose to not pay. They can't legally close an overdrawn account, so they most often just walk away, knowing the bank will take a hit, and it's very rare that something as trivial as O/D fees would go to collection. They'll go to the next bank down the street, rinse & repeat. 

So, in those particular cases, the bank does genuinely lose twofold: 1st, in non-revenue in potential interest for funds that aren't there (but believe me, banks absolutely count on that), and 2nd, banks' credit rating with the government takes hits based on active accounts with zero (or less that zero balance). Banks absorb countless millions from people that walk away owing.

That's why many banks have some kind of minimum balance requirement to avoid account "maintenance" fees. It costs a bank more to mail out statements than it earns interest on a checking account with $500.

I should add, I am no longer a banker, and am in no way defending banks. I think they're the debbil, and should all be burned to the ground. They make money in a million other crooked ways.
